title: Summit Fever
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: Macbeth (Shakespeare): ambition, power and tragedy
source: Written for english/y9 lesson 30 ('Summit Fever' (teacher-written article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 30: Non-fiction: when chasing goals harms judgement. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: Summit Fever
paras: Goals are supposed to help us. Yet research on decision-making suggests that a goal held too tightly can blind us. When people are fixed on a target, they notice less, take bigger risks and bend rules they would normally respect.

Mountaineers know this danger well: climbers sometimes push on towards a summit after their safe turnaround time, because they cannot bear to stop so close. The summit becomes more important than the climb down. The lesson is not to give up ambition, but to decide in advance what you will never sacrifice to reach it.

The same pattern appears far from any mountain. A company sets a target for sales so high that staff begin to mislead customers. A runner so determined to win that they ignore an injury until it ends their season. A pupil so desperate for a top grade that they copy an essay. In each case, the goal began as something good and became a master instead of a servant.

Psychologists sometimes call this 'goal fixation'. The closer we get, the louder the goal becomes, and the quieter everything else: our safety, our honesty, the people beside us. Being so close makes stopping feel like losing everything already invested.

Experienced climbers protect themselves with a simple rule: they agree on a turnaround time before they start, while their heads are clear, and they keep to it however close the summit looks. It is not a lack of ambition. It is ambition with a conscience.
So set your goals high. But write down, before you begin, the lines you will not cross on the way.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: A goal held too tightly can blind us; decide in advance what you will never sacrifice.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: The extended mountaineering example; a list of other cases; the contrast 'master instead of a servant'; expert terms ('goal fixation').

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: With an imperative instruction to the reader: set goals high but write down your limits.

questions.q: Retrieve the claim and two effects of goal fixation.
questions.a: Claim: a goal held too tightly can blind us. Effects: notice less; take bigger risks; bend rules.

questions.q: What is 'summit fever' in your own words?
questions.a: Pushing on to a goal past the safe point because you cannot bear to stop.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, explain how the writer persuades readers that goals can be dangerous. Use two methods. Starter: 'The writer argues that...'
questions.a: Claim plus two methods (research, extended example, advice) with effects.

questions.q: Extend: apply 'decide what you will never sacrifice' to Macbeth.
questions.a: Macbeth never decides; he sacrifices loyalty, sleep and peace for the crown.

questions.q: Stretch: is the article fair to ambition? Explain.
questions.a: Yes: it says ambition is not bad, only ambition without limits.

questions.q: What is the writer's main advice?
options: Decide in advance what you will never sacrifice
questions.a: C) Decide in advance what you will never sacrifice. The final sentence gives the advice; the article does not reject ambition.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: Yes, if we sacrifice our values to get it, as Macbeth does.
